panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: H&E-stained patient tumor tissue showing ganglionic/neural-crest tumor histology in the reported ROHHAD-associated intracranial tumor; includes an inset. B: Chromogranin A immunoreactivity in the patient's tumor supports a neuroendocrine neoplasm in the context of the ROHHAD case report. C: Synaptophysin immunoreactivity supports neuroendocrine differentiation in the patient's ROHHAD-associated tumor. D: SOX10 positivity with schwann-like cells supports neural-crest tumor histology; arrows annotate positive cells. E: CD45 immunostaining shows abundant immune cells/lymphocytic infiltrate within the patient's ROHHAD-associated tumor; feature is not in the configured vocabulary. F: Keratin-negative immunostaining is part of the immunophenotypic characterization of the patient's ROHHAD-associated intracranial tumor; negative staining alone is a weak visual finding.

There was no clear glial component of the tumor (OLIG2 and GFAP-negative) and no neuroblasts were found. The tumor could not be classified using methylation profiling. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial T2 MRI from a patient with ROHHAD syndrome showing the reported intracranial tumor; article title identifies an intracranial NET in ROHHAD. No listed vocabulary finding fits this imaging manifestation. B: Axial FLAIR MRI showing the same ROHHAD-associated intracranial mass with caliper measurements. No vocabulary finding matches this MRI tumor manifestation. C: Sagittal 3D FLAIR MRI demonstrating the large ROHHAD-associated intracranial tumor extending through the brainstem/cervical region. The caption explicitly notes no hypothalamic or pituitary abnormality, so classic ROHHAD MRI findings are absent.

panels.figure_caption: MRI images of the intracranial tumor. (A) T2 (B) MPR tra FLAIR (C) 3D FLAIR. Large hyperintense mass in right cerebellar peduncle, medulla oblongata, pons, cervical myelum. No hypothalamic or pituitary abnormalities are seen.
in_text_mentions: The MRI showed a large cerebellopontine mass suspect for a glioma (Figure 1). There were no abnormalities in the hypothalamic-pituitary region, the optic nerves nor signs of hydrocephalus on MRI. Ophthalmological evaluation showed normal eye motility and alignment; the optic nerves appeared normal although fundoscopy was difficult to perform. There were no new neurologic complaints. The tumor was not considered an explanation for her respiratory issues and also not for the development of obesity, for which reason the endocrinologist was consulted.

Caption and article title directly support the disease attribution.

panels.rationale: The figure shows a clinical photograph of a pediatric patient explicitly diagnosed with ROHHAD syndrome. The image and associated caption document several key features of the syndrome, including syndromic facial features, rapid weight gain, and signs consistent with autonomic dysregulation.

in_text_mentions: On physical examination, syndromic facial features were recognized, such as depressed nasal bridge, broad nasal tip and down-turned mouth (Fig. 1). Strabismus (eye misalignment), hepatomegaly, red and cold extremities, and livedo reticularis in the upper and lower extremities were also observed. Her pubertal stage was Tanner II, while the growth charts revealed short stature (< 3rd percentile for age and sex) and rapid weight gain after the age of 2 years (Figs. 2 and 3).

panels.attribution_text: Şiraz et al. ROHHAD Syndrome, a Rare Cause of Hypothalamic Obesity: Report of Two Cases. Journal of clinical research in pediatric endocrinology 2018. doi:10.4274/jcrpe.0027. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
in_text_mentions: evaluation or treatment was considered for GH deficiency, due to the patient’s normal height. However, a predisposition to neural crest tumor was considered despite the low IGF-1 and IGFBP3 levels of the patient. Brain and pituitary magnetic resonance (MR) imaging studies were found to be normal. The IQ score was 65. The pale appearance of the fingers was considered to be due to Raynaud’s phenomenon (Figure 1). Alterations in body temperature and Raynaud’s phenomenon were attributed to autonomic dysfunction. Pulmonary hypertension was detected on echocardiography and nifedipine was prescribed.

panels.rationale: The panel is a clinical photo of a child presented in a case report for ROHHAD Syndrome. The patient exhibits morbid obesity (BMI 30.4 kg/m2), which is a characteristic manifestation of the syndrome mentioned in the article and caption.
panels.attribution_text: Şiraz et al. ROHHAD Syndrome, a Rare Cause of Hypothalamic Obesity: Report of Two Cases. Journal of clinical research in pediatric endocrinology 2018. doi:10.4274/jcrpe.0027. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
in_text_mentions: for evaluation of obesity. The patient was reported to have sleep apnea and aggressive behavior. She was born at term, with a birth weight of 2800 g (-1.2 SD) and she had uncontrollable eating, starting at two years of age, with rapid weight gain. There was no consanguinity between parents and she had two healthy siblings. Body weight was 11 kg (±3.7 SD) and height was 101 cm (±1.7 SD) with a BMI of 30.4 kg/m2 (±5.7 SD) (Figure 2). The patient had central cyanosis. Blood pressure was 90/60 mm/Hg (95 percentile: 115/75 mm/Hg). Axillary body temperature measurements varied from 35.6 to 39.5 °C.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of a patient in the cohort (child) with ROHHAD syndrome. Panel A is stated to show a normal BMI at diagnosis, representing the initial presentation before or despite systemic issues. The figure is retained based on the cohort context. B: Clinical photograph showing a patient displaying excessive sweating, a recognized sign of autonomic dysregulation associated with ROHHAD syndrome, as stated in the caption.

in_text_mentions: association of fever and excessive sweating; panhypopituitarism; seizure in the context of hypothermia. Hospitalization following onset of the first symptoms occurred for three of four patients, median 3 months [3–3.1] prior to diagnosis. These three children were, respectively, hospitalized for hypernatremic coma, hypoxemic pneumonia, and prolonged unexplained fever with constant strabismus. These hospitalizations did not lead to the diagnosis of ROHHAD. The chronology of onset of clinical signs is summarized in Figure 1. The median body mass index was 17.4 kg/m2 [16.5–19.35] (Figures 2A–C).
